stem: While developing an application using the Anthropic API, a developer repeatedly encounters an HTTP 529 error during periods of high traffic. What does this specific error indicate, and how should the application respond?

options.text: It indicates an overloaded_error meaning Anthropic's API is temporarily overloaded; the application should retry the request with exponential backoff.
It indicates a rate_limit_error meaning the application has exceeded its allowed requests per minute; the application should prompt the user to upgrade their API tier.
It indicates an authentication_error meaning the API key is invalid or expired; the application must prompt the administrator to rotate the keys.
It indicates a request_too_large error meaning the prompt exceeded the context window; the application should automatically truncate the input text before retrying.

explanation: An HTTP 529 status code indicates an `overloaded_error`, which means Anthropic's API is temporarily experiencing high load. The recommended recovery strategy for this error type is to automatically retry the request using exponential backoff. This differs from a 429 `rate_limit_error`, which happens when the client exceeds their specific allotted rate limits.

distractorNotes.b: A rate limit error uses HTTP 429, not 529. While both might involve traffic limits, 529 is a server-side overload, whereas 429 is a client-side limit.
distractorNotes.c: An authentication error returns an HTTP 401. It is not related to high traffic or 529 errors.
distractorNotes.d: A request too large error returns an HTTP 413. It is caused by exceeding the token limit, not by periods of server-side high traffic.

sourceNote: Errors — HTTP 529 overloaded_error and retry strategies

stem: A developer is building a classification application with Claude. During initial testing, they notice the model occasionally outputs invalid categories. Which TWO foundational debugging steps should they take to diagnose and resolve this issue? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Review the model's outputs and adjust the prompt to explicitly define the allowed categories.
Lower max_tokens so the model cannot append explanatory prose after the category label it selects.
Retry any response whose label falls outside the allowed set, so the caller only ever observes a valid category.
Switch the API request from the Messages API to the legacy Text Completions API.
Add the failing examples to an evaluation test suite to systematically measure if prompt adjustments fix the issue.

explanation: When debugging unexpected model behavior such as incorrect categorization, foundational steps include reviewing the failures to refine prompt instructions (such as explicitly defining allowed categories) and adding those failing cases to an evaluation suite. A test suite allows developers to iterate on the prompt systematically, ensuring that changes resolve the errors without causing regressions.

distractorNotes.b: This truncates the response rather than constraining what it may say, and a label outside the allowed set is just as invalid when it arrives on its own.
distractorNotes.c: Retrying hides the defect behind added cost and latency without diagnosing it, and it produces no record that would show whether a prompt change actually helped.
distractorNotes.d: The Text Completions API is legacy. Switching to it is not recommended and will not inherently resolve instruction-following issues.

sourceNote: Develop tests — 'Tips for LLM-based grading' (rubrics and reasoning)

stem: A developer runs an exact-match evaluation to check if Claude correctly assigns one of four fixed labels to an input. The test continuously fails, despite manual spot-checks showing the model is generating the right words. What is the most appropriate first step to diagnose and resolve this test failure?

options.text: Inspect the raw outputs and update the evaluation script to normalize whitespace and casing before performing the exact match.
Replace the exact-match script with an LLM-as-a-judge prompt to flexibly evaluate the model's intended label.
Switch to manual human grading for all test cases, as automated string matching is too unreliable for categorical tasks.
Loosen the assertion to a substring match, so a label surrounded by extra words still counts as correct.

explanation: When an exact-match evaluation for categorical answers produces false negatives, a foundational debugging step is to inspect the raw output for trivial discrepancies. Anthropic's guidance highlights that code-based grading is the fastest and most reliable method for clear-cut answers, but it typically requires comparing the output "after normalizing whitespace and case." Replacing the check with an LLM judge or human grading fails to address the root cause and introduces unnecessary cost and latency for a deterministic task.

distractorNotes.b: An LLM judge adds cost, latency, and variance. It is suitable for complex or subjective judgments, not for evaluating fixed, categorical labels.
distractorNotes.c: Human grading is the slowest and most expensive evaluation method. The guidance explicitly advises avoiding it when a simple, automated string match is possible.
distractorNotes.d: A substring match would make the test pass, but it also accepts outputs it should reject: a reply that mentions one label while selecting another still matches. Normalising and keeping the exact match preserves the check's precision.

sourceNote: Develop tests — 'Grade your evaluations' (grading methods hierarchy)

stem: An engineering manager wants to monitor Claude Code usage across their team and verify that the telemetry pipeline is functioning correctly. Which statement accurately describes the fundamental approach to configuring and verifying Claude Code telemetry?

options.text: Claude Code automatically sends telemetry to Anthropic's central dashboard; administrators verify the pipeline by checking the Anthropic console for active developer sessions.

Telemetry is strictly opt-in; administrators must explicitly configure Claude Code to export to their own OpenTelemetry collector and verify the setup by observing standard metrics or events on their backend.
Telemetry is enabled by default in enterprise deployments; administrators verify the pipeline by ensuring the proprietary Anthropic monitoring agent is running alongside Claude Code.
Administrators enable telemetry by aggregating local log files from each developer machine; the pipeline is verified by running a standard Claude Code command to print a summary of recent sessions.

explanation: Claude Code's telemetry is opt-in and natively integrates with standard OpenTelemetry backends rather than phoning home to Anthropic or requiring proprietary agents. Administrators must explicitly enable it and provide OTLP endpoint details. The pipeline is then verified on the organization's own backend by checking for expected initial metrics (like session counts) or logs (like user prompt events) rather than relying on an Anthropic dashboard or local log scraping.

distractorNotes.a: Claude Code does not send organizational telemetry to a central Anthropic dashboard; it exports to the organization's own configured OpenTelemetry backend.
distractorNotes.c: Telemetry is never enabled by default, and Claude Code natively supports OpenTelemetry without requiring a separate proprietary monitoring agent.
distractorNotes.d: Telemetry is exported over the network via OpenTelemetry protocols, not by manually aggregating local log files or running local summary commands.

sourceNote: Monitoring usage — OpenTelemetry exporter setup and verification

stem: A developer is troubleshooting an FAQ assistant that gives significantly different answers when a user asks the exact same question in slightly different words. To systematically debug and measure this issue, which foundational evaluation criterion should the developer focus on?

options.text: Task fidelity, which evaluates whether the bot can identify a predefined correct answer.
Consistency, which evaluates how semantically similar the bot's responses are for similar types of input.
Relevance and coherence, which evaluates the logical flow and subsequence matching of the bot's summaries.
Tone and style, which evaluates subjective aspects like the bot's empathy and professionalism.

explanation: When a model provides different answers to paraphrased questions, it is failing the criterion of consistency. The documentation defines consistency as evaluating 'how similar do the model's responses need to be for similar types of input' and notes that 'similar questions should yield semantically similar answers, even if the wording varies.' Identifying the correct criterion is the foundational first step in debugging inconsistent model outputs. Task fidelity is used for clear-cut categorical tasks, relevance and coherence for summarization, and tone and style for subjective attributes.

distractorNotes.a: Task fidelity evaluates if the model produces a specific, clear-cut categorical answer, typically using exact match. It does not measure semantic similarity across paraphrased questions.
distractorNotes.c: Relevance and coherence is typically used for tasks like summarization to measure how well the output captures the core message of a reference text, not how well the model agrees with its own answers across different prompts.
distractorNotes.d: Tone and style evaluates nuanced, subjective aspects such as empathy, professionalism, or patience, which does not address the semantic agreement of the answers themselves.

sourceNote: Develop tests — 'Common success criteria' and 'Example evals' (Consistency)

stem: A nightly job that extracts fields from documents has started failing. On some runs the API returns a client error before the model is invoked; on others the call succeeds but the extracted values are wrong. An engineer wants to isolate where the fault lies before changing anything. What best separates the two cases?

options.text: Group every failure by HTTP status code, treating each 4xx as an integration fault and each 5xx as a fault in the model's output.
Separate failures the API rejected as invalid requests from calls that returned successfully, since the first class is the integration layer and the second is the output.
Compare the failure rate against the previous week, and treat any increase as a service-side regression that should be raised with the provider.
Retry the failures with backoff, and treat the ones that eventually succeed as transient so that the permanent failures are the ones investigated.

explanation: The two failure classes have different origins and different fixes. A request the API refuses never reached generation, so the fault is in how the integration assembled the call. A call that returns successfully but with wrong content did reach generation, so the fault lies in the prompt, the context supplied, or the handling of the output. Sorting by that boundary tells the engineer which half of the system to open first.

distractorNotes.a: Grouping by status does separate caller faults from service faults, but the wrong-value runs return 200 and so never appear in the grouping at all, and a 5xx is a service or transport fault rather than a defect in what the model produced.
distractorNotes.c: Rate comparison detects that something changed without indicating where, and it prematurely attributes the change to the provider rather than to the caller.
distractorNotes.d: Backoff is the right response to transient errors once identified, but it treats a whole mixed population as transient and hides the invalid requests it silently retries.

sourceNote: Errors — request-level errors versus response content
